$comment: What a book gets when it does not say otherwise. Change a value here to change every book that has not chosen for itself. A book that names its own size, theme or archetype in book.json wins. B5, studio and standard are the defaults this engine shipped with, and the books in books/ were laid out for them, so these three must not change casually.
$motionNote: Opt-in motion packs (see src/engine/motion/). Empty means a book gets no motion and builds byte-identical to before motion existed. A book names packs in book.json "motion": ["fade","draw"].

b5.note: ISO B5, the trim this engine was built for

b5-landscape.label: B5 landscape
b5-landscape.note: B5 on its side, for wide diagrams and timelines

a4.label: A4
a4.note: workbooks and manuals that live on a desk

studio.note: the default. Neutral, technical, one idea per page.

manual.label: Manual
manual.note: plain and procedural. Numbered steps you can follow.

reference.label: Reference
reference.note: dense and calm. For looking things up, not reading through.

atelier.label: Atelier
atelier.note: warm editorial, serif title. For essays and slow reading.

fontPacks.$comment: Opt-in script fonts. A book names packs in book.json "fonts": ["cjk-sc"]; build injects a link to each pack.css, which adds @font-face rules under the SAME family names the themes already use (Inter, Space Grotesk), with a unicode-range for that script. So no theme changes and, with no pack named, nothing changes at all. The woff2 files are fetched by `node src/engine/tools/fetch-fonts.mjs <pack>` and are not committed, which keeps the repo small; until they are fetched a page simply falls back to the system font for that script.

archetypes.$comment: An archetype is the SHAPE of a page, not its look. The theme decides how it looks, the size decides how much fits, and the archetype decides what is on it and in what order. Each shape below is written as an instruction to the drafter, so the same field is both the docs and the prompt. 'standard' must stay exactly as it was: it is the shape every committed book was written in, and it adds no data-archetype attribute, so its pages are byte-identical to what a model produced before archetypes existed.

standard.label: Standard
standard.note: one concept, one diagram, one action

procedure.label: Procedure
procedure.shape:
This page is a PROCEDURE. The reader is going to follow it, in order, probably for the first time.

  - The title is the verb: 'Add a webhook', not 'Webhooks'.
  - The explainer is a numbered sequence. Use <ol> inside <div class="explain">, one <li>
    per step, starting with the action and not the theory. Each step is one line
    the reader can do without rereading the previous one.
  - End the sequence with the thing that proves it worked, as its own <li>.
  - The diagram is the flow in order: boxes left to right, arrows between them,
    and the last box coloured teal for the outcome. A diagram of the individual
    steps as separate boxes is wrong here; the point is the order.
  - The action box is the first step, restated as something to do now.

recipe.label: Recipe
recipe.shape:
This page is a RECIPE. The reader is going to make this.

  - The title is the thing being made: 'Miso soup', not 'The idea of miso'.
  - The explainer has two parts, in this order and with nothing between them:
    first WHAT GOES IN, as a <ul> of concrete amounts or settings ('2 tbsp miso',
    'broth at 80C not boiling'); then HOW IT IS MADE, as numbered steps.
  - Do not put quantities in the steps. They are in the list above them.
  - The diagram is the sequence of stages from cold to done, each stage one box,
    arrows between, and anything that must not boil or must not overcook marked
    in red because it is the mistake a reader will actually make.
  - The action box is 'make it now', and it names the hardest single step.

exercise.label: Exercise
exercise.note: a task with a stated goal and a check
exercise.shape:
This page is an EXERCISE. The reader is being asked to do something. - The title is the task as an instruction: 'Add a rate limit', not 'Rate limiting'. - Open the explainer with the GOAL in one sentence, as a

with the class 'hl' on the key phrase, so the reader knows what they are aiming at. - Then the task, in numbered steps. Then the CHECK: the exact thing they will see, run or read that tells them it worked. - The diagram shows before and after: the same system once without the change and once with it, the failure in red on the left and the good outcome in teal on the right. - The action box is the check, not the first step. The check is what they leave the page with.

reference.label: Reference
reference.note: a table or list, kept dense on purpose
reference.shape:
This page is a REFERENCE ENTRY. The reader opened the book to find one thing and will close it again. - The title is the lookup key itself, spelled the way a reader would search for it, not the way the book would chapter it. - The explainer leads with the answer in the first sentence. No preamble, no 'let's explore', no history unless the history IS the thing being looked up. - Then a if there are fields worth comparing, or a
    if there is a closed list. The table's
states the answer outright. - Then at most two

for the caveat and the gotcha. Keep it dense. A reference page is allowed to feel short and still be complete. - The diagram is skipped if the page has a table. If you do include one, it shows the shapes of the thing, labelled, with no arrows.
